Issued at 230 PM CDT Sun Sep 27 2026

Cyclonic flow is found over the northern Plains this afternoon 
as a deep upper level low exits to the northeast out of the 
Canadian Prairies. A weak cold front slowly exiting to the
southeast of the forecast area continues to promote some 
isolated showers across portions of our south central. Overall 
rain accumulations are expected to be very limited to non
existent. Elsewhere clear skies are generally expected through 
the early to mid afternoon as a surface center of high pressure 
moves across the far northwest, before beginning to cloud back 
over as a second cold front associated with the Canadian Low 
beings to move in.

Late tonight into early Monday, a broad shortwave trough 
ejecting off a closed low over the western Canadian coast is 
expected to begin moving in the northern Plains. At the surface,
a low pressure center developing on the lee side of the rockies
is progged to be lifted up and across Wyoming into the Dakotas 
through the day, pushing an attendant warm front across 
southwestern through eastern North Dakota. At the same time, a 
moderately strong (50 to 60 knot) H7 jetstreak is expected to 
develop across south central into eastern North Dakota early 
Monday morning through Monday afternoon. With such ample sources
of lift across the area, and with moisture returns increasing 
up ahead of the developing low center, widespread medium to high
chances (60 to 90 percent). A fairly modest convective 
environment is also expected to develop by early Monday morning,
with model MUCAPE values peaking up to around 1000 J/KG and 
bulk shear values around 35 to 40 knots. An interrogation of 
BUFKIT model soundings through early Monday afternoon indicates 
that much of the predicted instability should be fairly elevated
about a robust cap, and above the better shear found below 1 KM
AGL. The questions remains what will occur as we head into the 
later portions of Monday afternoon as the H7 jet begins to kick 
in. While the majority of short term CAMs advertise the robust 
capping over North Dakota persisting through the day, one of two
of them do capture a storm or two becoming surface based by the
mid to late afternoon. In such a circumstance, an isolated 
stronger to marginally severe thunderstorm or two cannot be 
ruled out, with the area to watch being southwestern and south 
central North Dakota into the northern James River Valley. The 
primary hazards associated with any severe thunderstorm that 
does develop would be large hail up to the size of a quarter, 
and damaging wind up to 60 MPH. Of note is a potential window 
during which an isolated tornado would become possible, mainly 
in late afternoon into the early evening as the surface low 
lifts into central and eastern North Dakota. While predicated on
a surface based storm developing, the strong near surface shear
near the triple point of the low could promote near surface 
(0-1km) SRH values around 150-200 KM and decently curved 
hodographs across the southern James River Valley. While the 
overall potential of a tornado remains low as this time, we will
need to monitor forecast trends over the next 24 hours, 
especially if surface based storms become more likely. 

Otherwise, moderate to heavy rainfall can be expected across 
portions of western and much of western North Dakota starting 
late tonight through Monday night. With high PWAT values 
exceeding 1.5" by the late afternoon, the NBM probability of 
exceeding 1.0" of rain accumulation is high (70 to 90 percent) 
across much of central North Dakota, with a low chance (20 to 40
percent) to exceed 3.0" over portions of the James River 
Valley. With such high PWATs, moderate to heavy rainfall 
approaching at least 0.5" to 1.0" per hour can also be expected
where and when thunderstorms occur. As of this forecast cycle, 
the EFI highlights portions of central North Dakota for high 
values approaching 0.9-0.95 and a shift of tail values of 2, 
which indicates high confidence on an anomalously high 
precpitation event compared to our climatology. Of note is that 
a handful of CAMs capture training thunderstorm development 
along the warm front as it occludes over south central into 
northeastern North Dakota late Monday afternoon through Monday 
evening. If this scenario were to play out, localized flood can 
be anticipated despite the fairly dry, thirsty ground present
over much of central North Dakota.

Looking ahead to the remainder of the workweek, near zonal to 
southwesterly flow is anticipated over the northern Plains 
through at least Wednesday promoting relatively dry somewhat 
warmer weather with highs broadly in the mid 60s to mid 70s. By
